methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: A site with an explicit thesis needs unassailable numbers. This page documents every source, formula and limitation — and the code is open.

counter.title: The counter
counter.body: The counter estimates Brazil's tax revenue for the current year spread uniformly over time, in the same spirit as ACSP's Impostômetro: the estimated annual total is divided by the seconds in the year, producing a per-second rate applied to the time elapsed so far.
counter.formula: value(t) = (estimated annual revenue ÷ seconds in year) × seconds elapsed this year

costs.title: Reference costs
costs.body: Each equivalence uses a unit cost from an official source (or press coverage citing an official body). Values are rounded conservatively.

payroll.title: The salary calculator
payroll.body: The calculator applies the official 2026 tables: progressive INSS brackets (Interministerial Ordinance MPS/MF No. 13/2026, ceiling of R$ 8,475.55 and maximum deduction of R$ 988.09) and IRRF using the Federal Revenue's progressive table plus the reducer from Law No. 15,270/2025, which zeroes the tax up to R$ 5,000 of monthly income and phases out gradually up to R$ 7,350 (reduction = R$ 978.62 − 0.133145 × income). The IRRF base uses the greater of legal deductions (INSS + R$ 189.59 per dependent) and the simplified deduction of R$ 607.20.
payroll.irrfNote: The calculation covers CLT payroll deductions (INSS + IRRF). It does not include taxes embedded in consumption, which hit later, with every purchase. Sources:

limits.title: Known limitations
limits.item1: Actual revenue collection is not uniform across the year — the counter is an average; period totals converge to official figures.
limits.item2: Equivalences are illustrative: they compare total revenue with unit capital or consumption costs, without ongoing operating expenses (teachers, medicine, maintenance).
limits.item3: Current-year estimates are revised as official consolidated figures are published.

open.title: Open code and data
open.body: All of this site's code, data and formulas are public on {link}. Found a mistake? Open an issue — sourced corrections are welcome.

timeMachine.title: The Time Machine
timeMachine.body: Period totals use the Impostômetro/ACSP annual closings as verified milestones (2010, 2015, 2018, 2019, 2021–2025). Years without a public milestone are filled by linear interpolation between neighboring milestones, and the current year enters with its estimate prorated by elapsed time — periods containing any approximation are flagged on the page itself. Presidential terms use calendar years (transitions such as the 2016 impeachment are simplified to whole years). Accumulated inflation compounds IBGE’s annual IPCA for each year in the range (full series through 2025). The historical tax burden (1947–2024) uses confirmed milestones from three series: Ipea/Varsano (1947–1998), FGV/Ibre (1990–2024) and the Treasury (2010–2024); the 2007 GDP revision lowered the post-1995 series by ~2 p.p., and Treasury and FGV differ ~2 p.p. in current methodology — so we publish only textually confirmed points, each with its own source. Social indicators follow the same rule: only confirmed milestones (IBGE censuses, mortality tables, SIM/Datasus, PNAD Contínua), with series breaks flagged on each chart — unemployment, for instance, only has a comparable national series since 2012, and homicide milestones we could not verify at the source were left out.

archive.title: An archived copy of every source
archive.body: Official pages go offline, articles get edited, PDFs change address. So every source cited on the site has a copy in the Wayback Machine, recorded with its date in {link}. If the original link dies, the copy proves what the source said when the number came in.

footer.disclaimer: Impostossauro is an independent indictment of the entire political class, every party, measured with the same yardstick. Every number is sourced.

timeMachine.inflationLine: Since {start}, prices rose {pct}% (accumulated IPCA). The same money buys less and less — and the inflation is manufactured by the very State that promises to save you from it.

timeMachine.workDaysLegend: IBPT study "Days Worked to Pay Taxes": 149 days in 2025 (Tax Freedom Day on 5/29/2025), with 40.82% of average income going to taxes.
timeMachine.tiradentesConclusion: The Portuguese Crown charged the quinto: about 20% of all gold mined in Minas Gerais. When the annual quota of 100 arrobas fell short, came the derrama — the forced collection of the difference, at gunpoint. It was the threat of the 1789 derrama that triggered the Minas Conspiracy; Tiradentes was hanged and quartered on April 21, 1792. Today, the Brazilian state keeps 32.40% of everything the country produces and about 41% of the average worker's income — and the derrama is automatic: it's deducted from the paycheck and built into the price tag, no troops required.

inflationPage.title: The Inflation Factory
inflationPage.intro: Inflation is not a natural phenomenon. It's a government spending more than it collects and printing the difference. And the charge is double: after eroding your money, the State taxes the correction.

calc.title: The tax on nothing
calc.intro: You invest, the money grows, and part of that growth merely keeps up with the inflation the government itself manufactured. Yet the 15% income tax hits the entire nominal gain — with no inflation adjustment. Do the math:
calc.note: The default inflation of {pct}% p.a. is the geometric average of IPCA 2010–2025 (IBGE). Adjust as you like.
calc.punchLost: You LOST purchasing power — and still pay {tax} in tax on a "profit" that does not exist.
calc.punchGain: {share}% of your tax falls on pure inflation. Your real effective rate: {rate}% — not the advertised 15%.
calc.explain: The government creates the inflation, inflation inflates your nominal gain, and the tax hits the inflated number. The more inflation the government creates, the more tax it collects from you, on a gain that bought nothing.
calc.legalNote: Since Law No. 9,249/1995, Brazil does not allow inflation adjustment when computing capital gains: the 15% tax falls on the nominal gain.

currencies.title: The currencies the government has burned
currencies.intro: A serious country does not replace its currency. Brazil replaced it six times in 52 years — each swap marks a currency that inflation destroyed.
currencies.punch: From 1942 to 1994, the Brazilian government cut {zeros} ZEROS off the currency.

fallacies.title: The Debunker
fallacies.intro: When the math doesn't add up, a ready-made excuse appears: blame Portugal, the foreigner, the billionaire, the previous government. Here we do what politicians hate: the math, with sources.

gold.claim: Brazil is poor because Portugal stole our gold.
gold.statDocumented: tonnes with documented arrival in Portugal (1720–1807); total production estimated at 800–1,000 t.
gold.statValue: the value of ALL that gold at today's price (up to 1,000 t × ~US$ 4,375/oz).
gold.statDays: how long the Impostossauro took to swallow the same amount, at {year} pace.
gold.punch: An entire century of "colonial exploitation" equals one or two months of Brasília. Portugal left in 1822 — whoever has been charging the royal fifth on your life since then lives in Brasília.

hunger.claim: We took Brazil off the Hunger Map.
hunger.body: The detail nobody mentions: the yardstick was not the same in the two "exits". In 2014 the published line was 5% undernourishment — Brazil left at ~3%, a number that would fail today's 2.5% cutoff. And FAO recalculates the entire historical series with every report. The announced victory depends on which yardstick is used, and whoever writes the headline never shows the yardstick.
hunger.punch: Between one UN photo-op and the next, 48.9 million Brazilians remained below the poverty line (IBGE, 2024). Hunger does not read reports.

hunger44.claim: US$ 44 billion could end world hunger.
hunger44.body: In 2021 the UN World Food Programme put the cost of pulling 42 million people out of hunger at US$ 6.6 billion. When Elon Musk bought Twitter for US$ 44 billion, politicians lined up to be outraged: that money could have ended hunger. If money solves it, the math applies to everyone.
hunger44.statPlan: was the UN's plan to lift 42 million people out of hunger, in October 2022 reais.
hunger44.statRevenue: is what the Brazilian state collected in {year}, across all three levels of government.
hunger44.punch: Brazil collects {times} times the UN's entire plan, every single year — {days} days of revenue. And hunger is still here. Why does nobody ask that?

indicators.title: R$ {trillions} trillion later...
indicators.intro: That is what the Impostossauro ate in {years} years, according to the Impostômetro. With that mountain of money, any country becomes Switzerland. See what Brazil became:

illiteracy.label: Illiteracy (15 and older)
illiteracy.comment: It fell — over TWENTY-ONE years. There are still ~11 million Brazilian adults who cannot read this page. At a cost of trillions, the shame gauge only dropped by half.

homicides.label: Homicides per year
homicides.comment: Better than the peak — and a packed stadium of Brazilians still dies EVERY YEAR. Security is the most basic duty of any State; that is what taxes were supposedly for.

sanitation.label: Treated sewage
sanitation.comment: In 12 years, 14 points of progress. At this pace Brazil treats 100% of its sewage around 2060. Half the country's sewage still runs into rivers and beaches — in the 21st century.

pisa.label: Education (PISA, math)
pisa.comment: Stagnant since 2009, ~93 points below the OECD average — over 4 school years behind. Trillions in promises of education first bought this.

indicators.punch: Money was never missing. The numbers show a State that charges like Scandinavia, delivers little, and still asks for gratitude with the next promise.

fallacies.methodNote: All sources are linked on the cards. Criteria and limitations are documented.
fallacies.tldr: Politicians' favorite excuses, dismantled with arithmetic and sources.

journey.title: The Journey of ONE R$ 100 bill
journey.intro: Follow your money from work to inheritance. Taxes apply at successive stages: payroll, purchases, savings, property and succession. Each charge reduces what remains yours.

ghost.title: Before your salary even exists
ghost.body: Your boss doesn't pay just your salary. On every real of payroll he pays employer social security, FGTS, accident insurance, Sistema S, plus provisions for the 13th salary and vacations, with charges compounding on charges. The documented result: a CLT worker costs 1.7 to 2 times the salary you see. In the FGV/CNI study, with indirect costs, it reaches 3. Nearly a second salary of yours, eaten before the payslip exists.
ghost.question: If that money exists because you worked... why have you never seen it?

payslip.title: The payslip arrives with deductions
payslip.body: From what's left, INSS and income tax are withheld at source. You don't pay the tax: you receive whatever the government left. It goes first, you go second.
payslip.question: Did you ever authorize this automatic debit? Did anyone ask you?

spend.title: You spend — and pay again
spend.body: Groceries, medicines, energy and fuel include taxes such as ICMS, PIS/Cofins, ISS and IPI. Money already taxed through payroll is taxed again when spent.
spend.question: When prices go up you blame the store... but who takes a third of your purchase?

save.title: You invest — returns are taxed
save.body: Anything left? If you invest, income tax takes 15% to 22.5% of the yield, including the part that merely keeps up with the inflation the government itself created. Funds also have the come-cotas: a tax that serves itself twice a year without you selling anything.
save.question: Does it make sense to pay tax on a "gain" that only recovered what inflation ate?

house.title: You buy property — the bills continue
house.body: Bought a house? ITBI on the deed, without the government laying a single brick. Paid it off? IPTU comes due every year, forever. Bought a car? IPVA, every year, forever.
house.question: If you must pay every year to keep what's already yours... is it really yours?

inherit.title: You die — inheritance is taxed
inherit.body: Transferring assets to your children is also taxed: ITCMD can reach 8%, depending on the state and applicable rules. Money taxed through work, spending and building wealth faces another bill.
inherit.question: How many times can the SAME money be taxed before that deserves another name?

reflection.opening: You work. Your employer pays more than the amount shown as your salary. And the revenue that funds that payment is also subject to tax. It comes from customers whose money may already have passed through other charges.
reflection.title: The charges did not begin with your payslip. And they do not end when your salary arrives.
reflection.circulation: Money changes hands, becoming wages, purchases, investments or property. Having been taxed before does not prevent a new transaction from generating another charge.
reflection.spending: You shop with what is left. Tax is part of the price. You try to build a reserve. With taxable investments, part of the return also goes along the way.
reflection.building: You decide to build a home. There is tax on buying the land and materials, and charges on the construction work. You pay for every stage, take every risk and spend years paying it all off.
reflection.ownership: At last, the home is yours.
reflection.annual: But paying off the home does not pay off IPTU, Brazil's urban property tax. The bill returns the next year. And the year after. You have finished paying for what you built; the State keeps taxing it.
reflection.inheritance: Then you die. The property you spent a lifetime building passes to your loved ones — and that transfer can also generate tax.
reflection.effort: The work was yours. The sacrifices were yours. The risk was yours. At each stage, the State took a share.
reflection.question: In the end, how much of what you built is truly yours?

verdict.title: In the end, {pct}% of everything you generate is his.
verdict.body: That's IBPT's math for the average income: 149 workdays a year become tax. And the bar above didn't even count property tax, vehicle tax or inheritance. The real journey is worse than the animation.
verdict.note: The bar illustrates the average burden on income. Property and inheritance taxes have their own bases, beyond it.

journey.taxCountLine: Brazil has about {count} taxes, fees and contributions. See the main ones throughout a lifetime.
journey.tldr: Money passes through six stages of taxation — from work to inheritance.
journey.finale: How many times must the same real be taxed before it is enough?

manifesto.title: It is your money. Demand answers.
manifesto.tldr: For 30 years they've promised to end hunger, violence and ignorance. Trillions later — where is it?
manifesto.intro: This site is an indictment. Not of one party: of the entire political class, and of our own habit of applauding old promises as if they were news. Every government swore to lift Brazilians out of misery. The Impostossauro does one thing: it puts the promise next to the number and lets you conclude.
manifesto.not1: There is no pledge of neutrality. The position is explicit: against tax abuse and mismanagement of public money.
manifesto.not2: No party receives editorial protection. Documents and data determine what we publish.
manifesto.not3: A number does not become evidence just because it supports the argument. Its source, period and definition must be identified.
manifesto.not4: No cherry-picking to manufacture outrage. An isolated figure cannot replace a historical series or its context.
manifesto.not5: No campaign platform or request for votes. Accountability continues when the government changes.
manifesto.not6: No argument is beyond revision. If the documents contradict the accusation, the accusation must change.
manifesto.yes1: An indictment with data: 30 years of promises next to 30 years of official indicators.
manifesto.yes2: A public demand for accountability: the speech beside the delivery, before the next promise.
manifesto.yes3: Open code and data: found an error? Fix it — credibility is our only asset.
manifesto.yes4: A path to the source: read the document, check the calculation and reach your own conclusion.
manifesto.yes5: Making the bill understandable: charts, examples and explanations so anyone can check it and demand answers.
manifesto.yes6: A work open to correction: errors reported with supporting documents are reviewed, and changes stay on record.

parable.title: The air-conditioner parable
parable.intro: Whenever someone defends a new tax to "solve" a problem, remember this room:
parable.p1: The country is a cooled room. The equipment works and maintains the temperature.
parable.p2: A car crashes through the wall. The cold air escapes through the hole — corruption, waste, mismanagement.
parable.p3: The politician's solution? Install a SECOND air conditioner: raise taxes. The hole? Still there.
parable.punch: Raising taxes without fixing the wall doesn't cool the room — it just raises the power bill. Yours.

literacy.title: Why this site speaks in pictures
literacy.stat1: of Brazilians aged 15-64 are functionally illiterate: they can read, but cannot understand what they read (INAF 2024).
literacy.stat2: only — read with full proficiency. The rate has not moved in 23 years. Among the young it got WORSE: from 14% to 16% functionally illiterate.
literacy.body: Charts, prominent figures and direct explanations make public documents readable. Understanding the bill is a condition for holding those who spend the money accountable.
literacy.punch: There's an irony here: that number is also their work. Decades of education first in the speeches, trillions collected, and 9 out of 10 Brazilians can't proficiently read the contract they signed with the State. Who gains from that?

rules.title: Publication criteria
rules.rule1: Every claim has an identified source. Official documents, research and reporting are distinguished. Without a source, we do not publish.
rules.rule2: We point the finger with the document in hand. When speech and data disagree, we show both — and the conclusion is yours.
rules.rule3: The yardstick is the same for every government, no exceptions — PT, PSDB, MDB, PL. Swapping yardsticks depending on who is in power is exactly what this site calls out.
rules.rule4: Got a number wrong? It gets corrected in public, with the right source. The history stays in the repository.
rules.outro: All code, data and formulas are open on

business.title: The Brazil Cost
business.tldr: To pay you R$ 5,000, your boss spends over R$ 8,000. And the company paid taxes before that.
business.intro: The employee sees the payslip. The employer sees the rest: nearly a second salary in charges, tax on revenue before any profit exists, and a tax bureaucracy that eats 1,501 hours a year of a company's time. In the end, all of it lands on the shelf price and on the job that never gets created.

stats.title: The numbers behind why everything is expensive here
stats.punch: Employing costs double, producing costs an extra fifth of GDP, and merely understanding the rules burns over a thousand hours a year. Then they ask why Brazil does not grow.

business.methodNote: The estimate methodology and its sources are documented.
business.assaiMarginLegend: Seventy-four billion passed through the till; one per cent became profit. The rest paid suppliers, staff, power, rent, interest and tax. The company's release headlines GROSS revenue, R$ 80.6bn — what counts here is net revenue (R$ 73.8bn), which is the denominator of the margin and the same yardstick as the other two. Divergence on record: other sources cite R$ 930 million in profit, under a different accounting treatment (IFRS 16); we use the figure from the company's own release.

federalRevenueChart.rulerTitle: Why the line starts in {firstYear} and not in 1994
federalRevenueChart.rulerText: The tax authority has published this monthly series since 1994, and the file is in the repository. But social security revenue does not appear in it for 1994. In {firstYear}, the first year it does, it alone comes to R$ 35.1bn out of a R$ 119.1bn total — nearly a third. Splicing 1994 onto the rest would draw a step that is a change of definition, not of revenue. We would rather show one year less.
federalRevenueChart.caveatsNote: Every term since {firstYear} appears in full. Lula 3 is still in office; the series runs to {lastYear}, the last full year in the tax authority spreadsheet.

burden.sectionTitle: The tax burden since 1947: the line that only climbs
burden.sectionIntro: Brazil's oldest official series shows the State's share of everything the country produces. Empire, dictatorship, democracy: the regime changes, the currency changes, the century changes. The direction of the line does not.
burden.title: Gross tax burden, % of GDP
burden.subtitle: From {from}% of GDP in 1947 to {to}% today. The Brazilian state has more than doubled the slice it takes of everything the country produces.
burden.hint: Tap, hover, or Tab through the dots to see each milestone value and source.
burden.alt: Line chart of Brazil's tax burden as % of GDP from 1947 to 2025, with the military dictatorship period marked.
burden.note: The line uses the most official source available for each year: a historical reconstruction to 1988, FGV/Ibre from 1990 to 2009 and the Treasury from 2010 onwards. The dashed stretch is not an annual series — those are milestones, which is why it does not become a solid line. Sources:
burden.milestoneRuler: Varsano/Ipea series — a historical reconstruction, the only source that reaches the period
burden.divergenceTitle: Two official sources, two numbers — every year
burden.divergenceText: The line always shows the most official source for each year, but it is not the only one measuring this. FGV/Ibre calculates above the Treasury in EVERY year where both exist, and always in the same direction: the widest gap was in {year}, {pp} points of GDP. Nobody is wrong — it is methodology. Anyone quoting "the tax burden" without saying whose number it is has picked one of the two without telling you.

indicators.kicker: The little table of indices that matter
indicators.title: What 80 years of taxes bought
indicators.intro: From the first census with confirmed data until today: literacy, life expectancy, infant mortality, sewage, violence, unemployment. Brazil improved on almost everything — as did nearly every country over the same period. The real question is a different one: given everything that was collected, where should we be by now?
indicators.hint: Tap or hover the dots to see the year, value and source.
indicators.gdpTitle: And how much did the economy grow, era by era?
indicators.gdpIntro: Average real GDP growth per period, from the IBGE series. The tax burden rose in almost every era; growth did not.

signature.home: The money was never missing. The answer is.
signature.calculator: You work until {date} for the government. Until when does it work for you?
signature.timeMachine: Tiradentes died over less tax than what we accept today.
signature.inflation: Brazil has already cut 18 zeros off its currency. None was the size of the problem.
signature.fallacies: The excuse changes with each government. The bill arrives in all of them.
signature.manifesto: It's not left versus right. It's those who pay versus those who charge and don't deliver.
signature.methodology: Don't take our word for it: check. Every source is one click away.
signature.economics: There is no such thing as government money. There's yours, changing address.
signature.publicMachine: The money reached every corner of Brazil. The results did not.
signature.promises: The law said what it was for, and for how long. The same people who wrote it were the ones who changed both.
signature.world: Nineteen of these countries tax more than Brazil. All twenty-nine of them live longer.
signature.worldDuelLess: {pais}: takes {pontos} points of GDP less than Brazil — and lives {anos} years longer.
signature.worldDuelMore: {pais}: takes {pontos} points of GDP more than Brazil and lives {anos} years longer.

laffer.chartNote: Illustrative curve, drawn to explain the concept: the real shape varies by tax, country and era, and the peak is not precisely known. Nothing here is a rate recommendation.
laffer.alt: Hill-shaped curve: revenue rises with the tax rate up to a peak, then falls to zero at 100%.

zones.low: Down here the bite per real is small — but the country produces a lot, and the base grows. Revenue comes from activity, not from rates.
zones.top: The peak zone: each extra point of tax rate yields less and less, because part of the activity gives up, hides, or leaves.
zones.high: Past the peak: activity shrinks, smuggling says thanks — and the government collects LESS while charging MORE. Everyone loses, including the treasury.

laffer.low: At low rates, the tax per real is small. A larger volume of economic activity can broaden the tax base.

econ101.title: The economics class school skipped
econ101.intro: No jargon without translation, no curve without a drawing. The basics of economics that explain why more tax does not become more schools — and that every government, of every color, ignores when voting.
econ101.tldr: Taxes have a turning point: past it, raising the rate starts shrinking the revenue. This page explains that without jargon.
econ101.cigarrosPunch: A 71% tax rate didn't turn into revenue: it turned into smuggling. Charging too much is also a way to collect too little.
econ101.cigarrosIlegaisLegend: of cigarettes consumed in Brazil in 2022 were illegal
econ101.cigarrosSonegadosLegend: in taxes not collected, by the FNCP estimate
econ101.lafferTitle: Raising taxes does not always raise revenue
econ101.lafferLead: At a 0% rate, the government collects zero. At 100%, also zero: nobody works for free. Between the two ends there is a hill — and past the peak, raising taxes means lowering revenue. The official name is the Laffer Curve; the summary is: killing activity is expensive.
econ101.lafferHonesty: Nobody knows for sure — it depends on the tax, the country and the era, and economists have argued about it for decades. The hill in the drawing is illustrative, not a map of Brazil. What no serious person honestly disputes: both ends exist, and a country can be on the wrong side of the hill for a specific tax. That is why overtaxed cigarettes finance smuggling and import taxes that are too high create gray markets.
econ101.conceptsTitle: Four ideas that explain almost everything
econ101.conceptsIntro: None of them is an opinion: they are concepts from any introductory economics textbook. What is astonishing is how many public decisions pretend they do not exist.

inflationTax.title: Inflation is a tax nobody voted on
inflationTax.body: When the government spends more than it collects and the difference comes from the printer, prices rise — and your money buys less without any new tax passing through Congress. Those with bank investments protected themselves; those living on cash wages paid the whole bill. Brazil has lived the extreme version of this.

incidence.title: Whoever hands over the tax is not whoever pays it
incidence.body: The "company tax" does not come out of the owner's pocket: it enters the cost, becomes price, and comes out of yours. Every link in the chain passes on what it can. A politician promising to "tax only companies" is promising to tax your grocery cart through a middleman.

deadweight.title: Deadweight loss: what dies never shows up in statistics
deadweight.body: When the cost of existing formally becomes unbearable, the business does not open, the job is not created, the receipt is not issued. That activity that stopped happening enters no government spreadsheet — but it is missing from your neighborhood. Economists call it deadweight loss; in practice it is the bakery that never existed.

opportunity.title: Opportunity cost: every real has an alternative address
opportunity.body: There is no "government money": there is working people's money, having its destination chosen by whoever governs. Every wasted real was a real that could have been a hospital bed, a teacher, sanitation. The right question is never just "how much does it cost?" — it is "what stopped existing to pay for this?".

econ101.methodNote: Figures, sources and limitations are documented.
econ101.casesTitle: Brazil on the hill: three receipts
econ101.casesIntro: Documented cases of taxes moving reality — on both sides of the hill.
econ101.casesCaveat: Sales reacting to a tax cut do not prove total revenue went up: the Reagan case shows cuts rarely pay for themselves. The hill is not an excuse for any cut; it is the reason to do the math before touching any rate.
econ101.worldIntro: International comparisons with the ruler declared: the ones that hold, we publish; the ones that do not — like "we pay more than Sweden" — we explain why not.

profit.kicker: The profit that seems, and the profit that is
profit.title: The company earned billions. Almost nothing was left.
profit.intro: When a politician says "abusive profit", they are quoting revenue — the money that comes in before paying suppliers, wages, electricity, rent, banks and taxes. What is left at the end, the real profit, fits in a sliver. Here are companies you know, with the numbers they publish themselves.
profit.costs: Suppliers, wages, electricity, rent, interest and taxes
profit.perHundred: For every R$ 100 sold, R$ {value} was left as profit. The rest was gone before that.
profit.dvaTitle: Where the value the company created went
profit.dvaIntro: The DVA is a table every listed company publishes, showing how the value it created was split. It is the most honest X-ray of the division: government, workers, banks, and last of all, the owners.
profit.smallTitle: And those with no billions at all
profit.smallIntro: The shop owner down the street never makes a record-profit headline. They show up in the statistic of who shut down.

federative.title: The money arrived. So what?
federative.intro: Taxes leave your pocket, go up to Brasília and come back down split between states and municipalities. Everyone knows that part. The question almost nobody asks: after decades of money arriving, did the indicators of those who received it move? The answer here isn't ours — it comes from Ipea and the World Bank.
federative.tldr: Decades of transfers later, Ipea and the World Bank say they did not reduce the inequality they were meant to reduce. The problem was never the money arriving.
federative.dependencyIntro: Before asking whether it worked, look at the size of the dependency the system created.
federative.verdictIntro: The Constitution created these transfers to reduce inequality between regions (arts. 3 and 161). The question is whether the mechanism delivered what it promised. The answer does not come from this site: it comes from Ipea and the World Bank.
federative.honestyTitle: The map is right. Reading it wrong is easy.
federative.honestyIntro: Two things change how any "who pays whom" map should be read, and both come from official sources. Without them the figure above misleads — not because it is wrong, but because it measures less than it appears to.
federative.mapPending: The interactive per-state map — how much each received and how its indicators look — is under construction: the official per-state tables have not been verified at the primary source, and nothing goes in here without that.
federative.methodNote: Sources, divergences and limitations are documented.
federative.indicatorsIntro: We do not yet have all 27 states verified at the source — only the extremes, which IBGE published. They already say a lot.
federative.ratioTitle: How much comes back for every R$ 100 a state sends
federative.ratioIntro: Here is the calculation everyone wants to see — and the reason it starts fights. There are two honest rulers for measuring "return", and they give nearly opposite answers. We publish both.
federative.officialGapTitle: Nobody in government does this math
federative.mapIntro: Click a state: how much it sent to Brasília, how much came back, and how school, health and safety are doing for the people who live there. Every figure is sourced, and anything unverified shows up in grey.
federative.piauiTitle: The state that climbed most in HDI still has no sewage
federative.sanitationMetricLegend: % of urban households connected to the sewage network
federative.ipeaConclusion: The revenue-sharing system cannot equalise the states' fiscal capacity, nor reduce the inequality between them — which is the job the Constitution gives it.
federative.paraphrase: Our paraphrase of the study, not a literal quotation.
federative.paraphraseUnverified: Our paraphrase. The original document has not been opened yet — the server refuses automated access, and the check is queued.
federative.rowsUnverified: These three figures were not found in the text of the cited page — they are probably in a chart. The check is queued.

map.legendTitle: How much comes back for every R$ 100 sent
map.hint: Hover or tap a state to see how much it sent to Brasília, how much came back, and how the people who live there are doing.
map.stateNoData: We do not yet have both halves of this calculation verified at the source for this state. Without that, we do not publish.
map.indicators: How the people there are doing
map.hiddenSentTitle: Whoever “collected” it is not whoever paid it
map.hiddenSentText: The federal tax office assigns the tax to the company's head-office address, not to where the thing was produced or consumed. The ore leaves Pará, the soy leaves Mato Grosso, the tax lands in São Paulo. That is why the Federal District collects more than Minas Gerais with a fraction of the population: it is where the state banks and state-owned companies are headquartered. Reading this map as “who supports whom” is reading it wrong.
map.hiddenReceivedTitle: “Received back” here is only the state government's cash
map.hiddenReceivedText: This figure counts what the federal government transferred to the state government. It does not count what goes straight to city halls, nor pensions, nor federal civil-servant salaries, nor federal universities or hospitals. São Paulo receives 9% of direct transfers and 28% of everything the federal government pays in pensions — none of which appears here. That is why São Paulo's R$ 1.7 on this map and the R$ 7–10 from Gazeta do Povo's analysis do not contradict each other: they measure different things.
map.hiddenNominalText: Nothing here is inflation-adjusted. Comparing 2018 with 2025 in current reais overstates the growth — exactly the trap this site calls out on the Inflation page, and it would be ugly to fall into it here.
map.hiddenDependenceTitle: “How much comes back” is not the most useful question
map.hiddenDependenceText: A state can receive little relative to what it collects and still depend on nobody. The question that changes the picture is another one: how much of the state's budget comes from Brasília. In 2024, Amapá depended on the federal government for 57.4% of its revenue and Acre for 57.2%, while São Paulo depended for 4.9% and Rio for 5.9%. That figure is in each state's panel, calculated from the same official report.
map.dependence: Of the budget comes from Brasília

hidden.heading: What they don't tell you
hidden.intro: The figure above is correct and officially sourced. That does not mean it tells the whole story — and the missing part usually changes the conclusion.

revenueAudit.rulerTitle: This line is not a year-by-year measurement
revenueAudit.rulerText: The Impostômetro publishes milestones — the day the country passed R$ 2 trillion, R$ 3 trillion. It is not a measured annual series. The years between milestones were filled in with a straight line, and now show as hollow circles only where a published milestone exists. Where there is no circle, the point was calculated by us, not measured by anyone.
revenueAudit.sourceTitle: And the milestone itself is a private body's estimate
revenueAudit.sourceText: The Impostômetro belongs to the São Paulo Commercial Association, using IBPT methodology. It is a respected counter and it covers all three levels — federal, state and municipal — which is the most complete figure publicly available. But it is not audited official data, and the association has a public stance on the tax burden. We use it because no official consolidated three-level figure exists in time, and we say where it comes from.
revenueAudit.measuredTitle: Where official data exists, it is now in the repository
revenueAudit.measuredText: Only the federal share has official month-by-month measurement, and the tax authority publishes the whole series back to 1994. Checking ours against it corrected two things and confirmed one. It corrected 2013, published on a narrower ruler than every other year (R$ 1,100bn counts only what the tax office administers; the total was R$ 1,138.8bn), turning a definition change into a revenue jump. It corrected the reach: the series ran from 2013 to 2025 because the by-state file lacks the three components before that; it now runs from 1995 to 2025 on the same ruler. And it confirmed the rest: where the two sources overlap, they agree to within 0.05%.

promises.pageTitle: They Promised: the law that created the tax and the law that changed the promise
promises.kicker: The official text against the official text
promises.title: They Promised
promises.intro: Every new tax is born with a promise written into law: what it's for, and for how long. Here are both official texts, side by side — what the law said when it asked for the money, and what another law changed afterward. No opinion: just the articles, sourced.
promises.tldr: The law said what it was for and for how long. Then both changed — by another law, from the same Congress.
promises.methodNote: Legal texts, sources, and what's still being verified are documented.
promises.collectedNoteLegend: Figure from an institutional page that cites the Federal Revenue Service, not the Revenue Service's original document.
promises.cpmfConclusion: A contribution called provisional, with a thirteen-month deadline written into its own law, lasted eleven years — and when it ended, the government that defended its extension in 2007 governed three more years without it. What else is still provisional?

world.kicker: Brazil among the 30 that charge the most
world.title: Similar taxes. Different outcomes.
world.intro: Brazil belongs to the group of the 30 countries with the highest tax burden in the world. Inside that group it is not the one that charges the most — and it is not the one that spends the least on education and health either. Even so, it comes last in life expectancy, last in homicides and last in sanitation. Every number here carries its year and its source.
world.tldr: Brazil charges and spends in line with rich countries. What it delivers is the last place in the group.
world.hiddenNotTopTitle: Brazil is not the one that charges the most in this group
world.hiddenNotTopText: It ranks {pos} of {total} by size of the burden, from the largest to the smallest: {acima} of these countries keep a larger share of GDP than Brazil does. The simple average of the 30 is {media}% of GDP; Brazil's is {brasil}%. Anyone who came here to debunk the legend that Brazil taxes more than anyone in the world finds the debunking at the door — and the page does not depend on it.
world.hiddenGroupTitle: Sitting mid-table in this group is not charging little
world.hiddenGroupText: These 30 are precisely the ones that tax the most on the planet, and sitting mid-table is still a heavy burden. Brazil takes a bigger slice than {abaixo} of them — among these {exemplos}. The lightest in the group, {paisMenor}, takes {menor}% of GDP, nearly eleven points below Brazil's.
world.hiddenTwoNumbersTitle: There are two figures for Brazil's tax burden on this site
world.hiddenTwoNumbersText: On this page, inside the IBPT study, Brazil's burden is {ibpt}% of GDP with 2023 data — it is IBPT's own calculation. Elsewhere on the site it appears as {oecd}, which is Brazil against the OECD average, as measured by {fonte}. Different years and methods give different numbers, and neither of them is wrong. We would rather show both than pick the one that sounds better.
world.payIntro: The list below is the whole group, from the one that charges the most to the one that charges the least, with 2023 data. Brazil is not at the top of it.
world.payBrazil: of GDP is Brazil's tax burden in the study's table, with 2023 data.
world.payAverage: is the simple average burden of the 30 countries in the table. The arithmetic is ours, over the published figures.

world.payPick: Click any country on the list to put it in a duel against Brazil, right below.
world.receiveIntro: Here the ruler turns around. The question stops being how much the State takes and becomes what shows up in the life of whoever paid. In each row: Brazil's value, the year, the range of the others and the source.
world.outcomesIntro: These three do not measure budgets, they measure people. In all of them Brazil comes last in the group.
world.inputsTitle: And it is not for lack of spending
world.inputsIntro: These two measure how much goes in, not what comes out. Brazil spends in line with the group.
world.inputsCaveat: Spending is not results: the two numbers above say how much the country puts in, not what it got for it. That is why they are kept apart from the ones above.
world.worstTitle: Where Brazil really is the worst
world.worstIntro: Not everything is mid-table. In these three Brazil sits at the very edge, the bad edge — and none of them is about how much is charged, but about how it is charged.
world.irbesTitle: The summary from the people who run this calculation
world.irbesIntro: IRBES is an index by IBPT that combines tax burden and HDI to answer how much well-being each country returns for the tax it charges. Among the 30, Brazil came last.
world.irbesAuthors: {edicao} edition, published on {publicado}, with data from {ano}. The study is signed by: {autores}.

justifications.sectionTitle: That was the reason given. And then?
justifications.sectionIntro: The section above sets two official texts against each other: what the law promised and what the law became. Here the clash is different — the reason the government gave for charging, against the indicator for the SAME period. The reason is theirs, the indicator is official, and the conclusion is yours.
justifications.pendingNote: There are cases already researched that have not gone in: they are waiting on the indicator document, and a case without an opened document does not appear here.

purchasingPower.title: The same basket, and how much of your time it costs
purchasingPower.intro: Reais in 2010 and reais in 2025 are different currencies: comparing the two figures says nothing. What crosses inflation without needing an index is time — how many hours you work to eat the same thing.

purchasingPower.noteLegend: From {first} to {last}, R$ 100 kept under the mattress became R$ {left}. R$ {lost} vanished without anyone taking anything out of your wallet — it is the tax that passes through neither law nor vote. Source:

purchasingPower.hoursIntro: São Paulo's basket in December of each year, measured in hours worked on the net minimum wage. Same capital, same survey, same yardstick — the bar is the time.

whatItBuys.title: What could it buy?
whatItBuys.tldr: One year of tax, stacked in R$ 1 coins, reaches the Moon twenty times over. This page measures the size of what leaves your pocket.
whatItBuys.intro: One year of tax in Brazil is a number nobody can picture. This page exists to give it size: dozens of things, each with a price, a source, and the provenance of that price declared. Buying is not running — and that is written here at the same size as the rest.
whatItBuys.purposeTitle: What we want out of this
whatItBuys.purpose1: The indictment is the start, not the conclusion. The site puts the official number next to the words of whoever produced it and points the finger. You draw the conclusion.
whatItBuys.purpose2: What we want is a layer of common sense. A country where voters have spent three decades applauding the politician who promised to lift them out of poverty, and where the political class changes its speech every even-numbered year, needs people who check before they clap.
whatItBuys.purpose3: This site does not say who to vote for. It says what the previous promise cost, with the source beside it.
whatItBuys.purpose4: If you got this far, do the one thing this site asks: share the number with the source attached.
whatItBuys.purposeLink: The full argument is in the Manifesto
whatItBuys.stickyLabel: is what Brazil collects in tax in one year — the {year} projection across all levels of government. This is the money buying every item below.
whatItBuys.physicalTitle: And if it were real money, in metal and paper?
whatItBuys.physicalIntro: The same year of taxes, at three different scales. Measurements and sources sit beside each calculation; the images are illustrative.
whatItBuys.moonTrips: {trips} trips to the Moon, back to back.
whatItBuys.earthLine: That same stack would go {laps} times around the equator.
whatItBuys.caveatKicker: What this page is not saying

whatItBuys.homeNumberDisney: times the whole of Disney, at its August 2026 market value
whatItBuys.homeNumberMoon: trips to the Moon, if the money became stacked R$ 1 coins
whatItBuys.homeSubtema: The same money, three answers. None of them is what happened.

privacy.title: Your privacy, with explicit rules.
privacy.intro: No accounts, advertising, cookies or sale of data. This policy explains local processing, hosting and visit counting.
privacy.updated: Version of 10 September 2026. The change history lives in the repository.

collected.title: What is collected
collected.p1: Salary and dependents are processed in your browser, without being sent to the project or analytics service. There are no accounts, comments or newsletters.
collected.p2: The site sets no cookies and loads no third-party analytics scripts. The home page counter loads an image through GitHub Camo; technical data from that connection is explained below.

local.title: What stays in your browser
local.p1: The browser stores your theme, the chosen currency and the beta notice dismissal, until you clear site data. These preferences are not sent to any server.

hosting.title: Hosting
hosting.p1: GitHub Pages serves pages and logs IP addresses for security, as its documentation states. GitHub processes these logs under its own policy, including retention and international processing. The project does not receive these access logs.

analytics.title: Page view counting
analytics.on1: Each entry to the home page, including reloads and returns through site navigation, loads the Komarev counter image through GitHub Camo. The counter adds image requests without distinguishing unique people. The image uses a public identifier exclusive to this site, without salary, dependents, page query parameters or the referring address. The displayed total comes from the service when the image loads; it does not depend on publishing the site again.
analytics.on2: GitHub receives the IP address and technical connection data and retrieves the image from Komarev. According to the Camo documentation, this intermediary hides browser details from the image server. Komarev’s public code records the counter identifier and access times; it is not a personal browsing history. The project does not control these providers’ infrastructure logs or retention. Caching, blockers and outages can affect counting; opening the image URL outside the site can also increase it.

external.title: Links out
external.p1: Sources, GitHub, WhatsApp, X and Buy Me a Coffee open external services when clicked. Their policies apply there. Site fonts and illustrations are local; the counter image is loaded through GitHub Camo as described above.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.p1: The LGPD provides rights of confirmation, access, correction and deletion, according to the processing performed. Since the site keeps no data that identifies you, there is no record of yours to consult or delete. General questions may be raised on GitHub; do not post documents or personal data in issues. For data protection guidance and petitions, consult

changes.title: Changes to this page
changes.p1: Changes are dated in the public repository. If the site ever starts processing data that identifies you, this page changes first, and that processing will depend on your consent.

terms.title: What you can expect from this site — and what you cannot.
terms.intro: Short terms, because the site is simple: public information, open code, no charge. By using the site you agree to what is written here.

nature.title: What this site is
nature.p1: An indictment site about taxes and mismanaged public money, made by one person, with no party, no sponsor and no ads. The texts are the author's opinion, backed by the numbers and documents cited beside each one. It is not both-sides journalism and never claimed to be neutral.

notAdvice.title: What this site is not
notAdvice.p1: It is not financial, legal, accounting or tax advice. The calculator applies the official tables cited in the methodology to give an order of magnitude; it does not replace your accountant, the tax authority or your payslip. The counter at the top is an estimate, and the page says where it comes from.

sources.title: Sources and errors
sources.p1: Every number has a linked source, and paraphrase is flagged as paraphrase. Even so, a number can be wrong: a revised source, a misreading, a redone sum. When that happens, the correction is public, in the repository. Check the source before using a number from here against someone — that is what the site is for.
sources.p2: Content may be corrected and the service may be interrupted. These limitations do not remove rights or responsibilities established by law.

content.title: Use of the content
content.p1: The code is open under the MIT license. The site's texts and charts may be shared, quoted and reproduced, as long as the link to the page and the original sources come along. The data belongs to the public sources cited on each number. Quotes from politicians are reproduced from public documents and outlets, with credit.

links.title: Third-party links and services
links.p1: Sources, GitHub, WhatsApp, X and Buy Me a Coffee belong to third parties. The site neither controls nor answers for their content, availability or policies. Support through Buy Me a Coffee is voluntary, processed by them, and buys no content, removal or change of anything.

law.title: Law and contact
law.p1: Brazilian law applies, including the Internet Civil Framework and the LGPD. Content errors and general questions can be reported on GitHub. Do not post documents or personal data in issues.

spending.pageTitle: They spent it — where public money went
spending.title: They collected the taxes. What did they deliver?
spending.intro: Stalled works, inflated budgets and a community funding its own bridge. Documents show where some of the money went and where services failed to arrive.
spending.tldr: Paying tax is mandatory. Delivery must be demanded.
spending.scope: Selection checked on September 8, 2026. Each case states its period and what its figure measures. There is no grand total: stalled works, corrected budgets and community investment measure different things.
spending.conclusion: Taxes reach the treasury. Services must reach the public.
spending.share: They collected the taxes. What did they deliver? Stalled works and public spending, with documents on Impostossauro.
spending.machineCta: Works, advertising, political funds, appointed posts, payroll, state companies and government cards: see the documents.

stalled.title: Work started. The service never arrived.
stalled.metric: federally funded works at a standstill
stalled.body: TCU mapped 22,621 works: 11,469 were stalled, or 50.7%. Health and education accounted for 8,053. Schools, nurseries and care remained undelivered.
stalled.ruler: TCU’s mapped universe in April 2025. This counts works, not a total amount of money lost.

dnit.title: The budget shrank when someone checked it.
dnit.body: Ten DNIT tenders needed revision. TCU reported that a 60-centimetre culvert was entered as 60 metres, inflating one budget by R$8 million.
dnit.ruler: R$264 million is savings after correction, not money already diverted. The R$8 million is part of the audit, not an additional total.

fiscobras.title: Fifteen works with serious indications in an audit of twenty-five.
fiscobras.body: TCU found deficient projects and overpricing. The consolidated October 2025 report recommended halting one work.
fiscobras.ruler: Selection was based on risk and materiality, not a sample of all Brazilian works. These are indications. The DNIT audit above belongs to the same programme.

bridge.category: Community funding · Rio Grande do Sul
bridge.title: The community had to fund its own crossing.
bridge.body: Residents and businesses rebuilt the bridge from Nova Roma do Sul to Farroupilha. It reopened on January 20, 2024, 138 days after its collapse. Daer was still preparing the state’s preliminary design in February.
bridge.ruler: About R$6 million reported by Estadão; no audited final accounts were available in this research. The community crossing is 120 m; the state project specified 180 m, two lanes and shoulders. They are different projects.
